lines.text: Picture pytest starting up inside a glass box. It starts Python. Python starts a worker. Every one of them is born inside the box, and none of them can climb out.

lines.text: Why does that part matter? It's all one command.

lines.text: Because a fence around only the first program would be easy to step around: start something new, and the new thing is free. Here the operating system holds the line. On macOS the fence is called Seatbelt, on Linux it's bubblewrap, and anything a fenced program starts stays inside the same fence.

lines.text: So it's a blocklist of dangerous commands.

That's where it breaks. A blocklist cares what a command is called. The glass doesn't. It limits what the running process can reach, whatever the process turns out to be, so a harmless-looking command gets exactly the same box as a scary one.

Same idea, different defaults. In Codex, in workspace-write mode, commands write to the workspace, but the .git folder is kept read-only, and the network is off unless you turn it on.
